title: Hadith Knowledge
description: A question bank on hadith terminology, collections, selected authentic teachings, responsible transmission and contextual understanding, with explanations and references. Introductory terminology follows mainstream Sunni hadith scholarship.
difficultyMethod: Editorial classification; not calibrated from learner response data. Advanced means greater reasoning depth within this subject, not a scholarly qualification.

review.referenceCheck: Primary-text references checked during preparation; this is not independent scholarly approval.

selectionHints.unknownResponse: Handle I am not sure as a UI action, not as a fifth answer option.

questions.question: Which description best fits a prophetic hadith?

options.text: A transmitted report about the Prophet's words, actions, approvals or characteristics
Any inspiring statement shared by a Muslim
Only a verse of the Quran
Any later scholar's legal opinion

questions.explanation: Prophetic hadith report the Prophet's teachings and life; an inspiring saying alone does not establish prophetic attribution.

references.label: Sunnah.com: About Hadith; sources and numbering

questions.question: What is an isnad in hadith study?

options.text: The English title of a chapter
The chain of transmitters
The printed page number
The legal ruling derived by a reader

questions.explanation: An isnad identifies a report's transmitters.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: What is the matn of a hadith?

options.text: The publisher's address
The chain of transmitters
The report's text or content
The translator's biography

questions.explanation: Matn refers to the transmitted content, as distinct from its chain.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: What does sahih mean as a hadith grade?

options.text: Fabricated
A translation into Arabic
A report without any attribution
Sound or authentic

questions.explanation: Sahih is an authenticity classification.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: What does hasan commonly mean as a hadith grade?

options.text: Good or fair, within the accepted categories
Definitely fabricated
A chapter title rather than a grade
Necessarily stronger than every sahih report

questions.explanation: Hasan is an accepted grade below sahih in the basic classification.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: What does daif mean in hadith classification?

options.text: Mass-transmitted
Weak
A Quranic verse
Automatically fabricated

questions.explanation: Daif denotes weakness; it is not simply another word for fabricated.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: What does mawdu mean when applied to a report?

options.text: Sound in itself
A translation footnote
Fabricated
A narrator's birthplace

questions.explanation: Mawdu denotes fabrication.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: Who compiled Sahih al-Bukhari?

options.text: Imam Malik ibn Anas
Imam al-Nawawi
Ibn Kathir
Imam Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari

questions.explanation: The collection is named after its compiler, Imam al-Bukhari.

questions.question: Who compiled Sahih Muslim?

options.text: Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj
Imam Abu Hanifah
Imam al-Tabari
Ibn Hisham

questions.explanation: Sahih Muslim is the collection compiled by Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj.

questions.question: Which companion narrates the hadith on intentions at the beginning of Sahih al-Bukhari?

options.text: Abu Hurayrah
Umar ibn al-Khattab
Anas ibn Malik
Abdullah ibn Abbas

questions.explanation: The opening hadith is transmitted from Umar ibn al-Khattab.

questions.question: According to Sahih al-Bukhari 1, what is central to the value of an action?

options.text: The number of people watching
The action's popularity online
The person's intention
The amount of praise received

questions.explanation: The hadith connects deeds and their reward with intentions.

questions.question: What does Sahih al-Bukhari 110 warn against?

options.text: Learning the name of a narrator
Asking for a source
Comparing two translations
Intentionally lying about the Prophet

questions.explanation: The warning concerns deliberately attributing falsehood to the Prophet.

questions.question: What conduct is warned against in Sahih Muslim 5, in the Introduction?

options.text: Narrating everything one hears
Checking a report before passing it on
Declining to share an unverified claim
Asking a knowledgeable person for help

questions.explanation: The narration cautions against passing on everything heard without discrimination.

questions.question: According to Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, how should a believer approach speech?

options.text: Say whatever attracts attention.
Say what is good or remain silent.
Repeat every rumour immediately.
Treat silence as always forbidden.

questions.explanation: The hadith joins responsible speech with care for neighbours and guests.

questions.question: In Sahih al-Bukhari 6114, who is truly strong?

options.text: The person who always wins an argument
The person with the loudest voice
The person who controls themselves when angry
The person who never accepts correction

questions.explanation: The hadith shifts attention from defeating others physically to self-control in anger.

questions.question: What repeated advice did the Prophet give the man in Sahih al-Bukhari 6116?

options.text: Always answer an insult immediately.
Never listen to advice.
Make others afraid of you.
Do not become angry.

questions.explanation: The man repeatedly requested advice, and the Prophet repeated the warning concerning anger.

questions.question: According to Sahih al-Bukhari 6464, which deeds are especially beloved to Allah?

options.text: Those maintained regularly, even if small
Only those done once before a large crowd
Only those that cause complete exhaustion
Those done solely to win praise

questions.explanation: The narration emphasizes sustained deeds, even when modest in quantity.

questions.question: Which lesson accompanies the Prophet's kissing of his grandson in Sahih al-Bukhari 5997?

options.text: Affection toward children is a weakness.
Mercy toward others matters.
Public dignity requires rejecting children.
Only adults deserve tenderness.

questions.explanation: The narration responds to a man's lack of affection toward his children with a warning about withholding mercy.

questions.question: Which teaching approach appears in Sahih al-Bukhari 69?

options.text: Make learning deliberately inaccessible.
Drive learners away with unnecessary harshness.
Make matters easier and give encouraging news.
Withhold every explanation from beginners.

questions.explanation: The instruction joins facilitation with encouragement and warns against making people averse.

questions.question: What blessing is mentioned in Sahih al-Bukhari 71 for someone for whom Allah intends good?

options.text: Automatic knowledge of every future event
Freedom from the need to learn
Guaranteed public fame
Understanding of religion

questions.explanation: The narration links intended good with understanding religion.

questions.question: How does Sahih al-Bukhari 100 describe knowledge being taken away?

options.text: Through the deaths of knowledgeable scholars
By every book disappearing simultaneously
By every learner forgetting all words overnight
Through the invention of page numbers

questions.explanation: The report describes scholars dying and uninformed leaders then giving answers without knowledge.

questions.question: Which conduct is named among the signs of hypocrisy in Sahih al-Bukhari 33?

options.text: Returning what was entrusted
Betraying a trust
Keeping a promise
Speaking truthfully

questions.explanation: The narration names lying, breaking promises and betraying trusts as signs requiring serious self-examination.

questions.question: In Sahih al-Bukhari 52, which bodily organ is used to explain the importance of inner soundness?

options.text: The hand
The ear
The heart
The foot

questions.explanation: The hadith links the soundness or corruption of the whole body with the heart.

questions.question: Besides clearly lawful and clearly unlawful matters, what does Sahih al-Bukhari 52 describe?

options.text: A category decided only by popularity
Actions beyond all moral evaluation
A rule that uncertainty makes everything forbidden forever
Doubtful matters not known by many people

questions.explanation: The narration identifies doubtful matters and counsels care in protecting one's religion and honour.

questions.question: In the hadith of Jibril in Sahih Muslim 8a, who is the visiting questioner ultimately identified as?

options.text: Jibril
A merchant seeking payment
The ruler of Persia
An unnamed enemy commander

questions.explanation: The Prophet explains that Jibril came to teach the companions their religion through the exchange.

questions.question: In the hadith of Jibril, how is ihsan explained?

options.text: Worshipping only when other people watch
Worshipping Allah as though seeing Him, knowing He sees you even though you do not see Him
Knowing the date of the Hour
Avoiding all questions about religion

questions.explanation: The explanation concerns awareness of Allah in worship, not public display.

questions.question: Which expression best captures nasihah in Sahih Muslim 55a?

options.text: Insulting someone to win an argument
Public humiliation as a goal
Sincere commitment and counsel
Indifference to others' wellbeing

questions.explanation: The narration describes religion through nasihah and identifies those toward whom it is directed.

questions.question: In Sahih Muslim 2564c, what does Allah look at rather than people's appearance and wealth?

options.text: Their clothing brands
Their family names alone
Their public follower counts
Their hearts and deeds

questions.explanation: The narration joins the heart with deeds, rather than making outward status the measure.

questions.question: In Sahih Muslim 2699a, what is promised for taking a path in search of knowledge?

options.text: Allah facilitates a path to Paradise.
The learner becomes incapable of error.
The learner no longer needs sincere intentions.
Every difficult question becomes instantly obvious.

questions.explanation: The report encourages seeking knowledge and also describes mutual help and gatherings of learning.

questions.question: In Sahih al-Bukhari 112, what did the Prophet instruct when a man from Yemen asked for the address in writing?

options.text: Destroy every written record of the address.
Have the address written for him.
Refuse because writing could never preserve teaching.
Replace the address with a poem.

questions.explanation: The report includes a specific instruction to write the address for the man.

questions.question: A message gives only a hadith number, without naming a collection. What is missing for a usable citation?

options.text: The sender's favourite colour
A count of how many times it was forwarded
The collection and enough details to identify the report
A decorative Arabic border

questions.explanation: A number identifies a report only within a reference system; the collection must also be known.

references.label: Sunnah.com: About Hadith; sources and numbering

questions.question: Two editions use different numbers for apparently the same hadith. What is the most sensible next step?

options.text: Declare both reports fabricated immediately.
Assume the larger number is more authentic.
Choose whichever number is easiest to memorize.
Compare the collection, wording and numbering systems.

questions.explanation: Numbering can differ between editions and arrangements.

references.label: Sunnah.com: About Hadith; sources and numbering

questions.question: A report appears in a hadith collection. Does its presence alone establish that it is authentic?

options.text: No; collections have different inclusion criteria, so the report's status must be checked.
Yes; every collection includes only authentic reports.
Yes; printing a chain guarantees soundness.
No; no written collection can preserve authentic reports.

questions.explanation: Inclusion and authentication are separate questions.

references.label: Sunnah.com: About Hadith; sources and numbering

questions.question: A page contains a hadith followed by an editor's explanation. What should be done before quoting both as the Prophet's words?

options.text: Keep everything inside one prophetic quotation.
Separate the transmitted text from the explanation.
Treat the editor as a companion automatically.
Assume every sentence on a hadith page has the same speaker.

questions.explanation: Only the report's actual wording should be represented as its transmitted text.

references.label: Sunnah.com: About Hadith; sources and numbering

questions.question: Sahih al-Bukhari 3461 encourages conveying even a small amount. Which clause in the same report prevents using this as permission to invent material?

options.text: A promise that popularity authenticates every saying
An instruction to omit every source
Its warning against deliberately lying about the Prophet
A statement that good intentions change invented words into hadith

questions.explanation: Encouragement to convey teaching appears alongside a grave warning against false attribution.

questions.question: Someone uses the hadith on intentions to argue that a good motive makes any method acceptable. Which assessment is most careful?

options.text: A sincere motive automatically makes all methods lawful.
Only public actions need intentions.
The hadith says actions have no importance at all.
The hadith establishes the importance of intention; it does not by itself authorize every method.

questions.explanation: A principle about intention should not be expanded into an unrestricted permission absent from the text.

questions.question: A moving religious story arrives without a source. Which response best follows the warning against narrating everything heard?

options.text: Pause and verify its attribution before sharing it as hadith.
Share it because it produced tears.
Add a hadith number from an unrelated report.
Assume a religious image proves its origin.

questions.explanation: Emotional impact does not establish whether the Prophet said something.

questions.question: Someone interprets the instruction about anger as saying moral strength means overpowering opponents. Which related narration most directly corrects this?

options.text: The report identifying the number of sacred months
The narration defining strength as self-control when angry
The narration about writing for Abu Shah
The report about migration intentions alone

questions.explanation: Reading the anger advice with the description of strength emphasizes restraint rather than domination.

questions.question: A Muslim breaks a promise, and someone cites Sahih al-Bukhari 33 to declare them outside Islam. What conclusion does the cited narration directly support?

options.text: Every broken promise automatically proves disbelief.
Only non-Muslims can ever break promises.
Promise-breaking is a serious hypocritical trait; the report alone does not establish that person's exclusion from Islam.
The report makes honest repentance impossible.

questions.explanation: The warning identifies dangerous conduct; judging a particular person's faith requires more than this isolated observation.

questions.question: Someone says the hadith about hearts means conduct never matters. Which part of Sahih Muslim 2564c challenges the claim?

options.text: It says wealth is the only criterion.
It says all intentions are equally sincere.
It excludes every outward action from consideration.
It explicitly mentions deeds alongside hearts.

questions.explanation: The report does not contrast the heart with moral responsibility; it names hearts and deeds together.

questions.question: After reading Sahih al-Bukhari 100, what should a learner avoid when asked a religious question beyond their knowledge?

options.text: Giving a confident ruling without knowledge
Admitting uncertainty
Referring the question to a qualified scholar
Continuing to learn

questions.explanation: The narration warns of uninformed leaders who answer without knowledge and mislead themselves and others.

questions.question: A person uses the encouragement of small regular deeds to justify abandoning obligations. What is the best reading?

options.text: Small voluntary deeds automatically replace all duties.
The narration praises consistency; it does not itself cancel obligations.
Any action is acceptable if repeated often.
Only the size of an action matters, never its regularity.

questions.explanation: The praise of sustained deeds should not be made into an exemption that the narration does not state.

questions.question: What feature of the hadith of Jibril shows that questions can serve a teaching purpose?

options.text: The companions were forbidden to learn from the exchange.
The questioner was praised for concealing every answer.
The Prophet identifies the questioner's visit as teaching the community.
The encounter made explanation unnecessary.

questions.explanation: The exchange models instruction through questions and answers, followed by clarification of the visitor's identity.

questions.question: A person treats the instruction to speak good or remain silent as a ban on all beneficial speech. What has been overlooked?

options.text: The hadith commands continuous talking.
The hadith applies only to business records.
The hadith says silence changes falsehood into truth.
Speaking good is itself one of the options the hadith gives.

questions.explanation: Responsible speech includes useful good speech; silence is not presented as the sole acceptable action.

questions.question: Someone claims no prophetic teaching was ever written during the Prophet's lifetime. Which report directly challenges this absolute claim?

options.text: The instruction to write an address for a man from Yemen
The report about controlling anger
The report about regular deeds
The report about welcoming a guest

questions.explanation: The specific writing instruction is enough to disprove the claim that there was never any writing at all.

questions.question: A chain contains accurate, trustworthy narrators. Is that fact alone sufficient to establish sahih status?

options.text: Yes; no other condition exists.
No; continuity and freedom from disqualifying anomaly or hidden defect also matter.
Yes; an attractive meaning supplies every missing condition.
No; trustworthy narrators can never transmit a sound report.

questions.explanation: All relevant conditions matter.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: A specialist says a particular chain is sound. Which further claim should not be assumed automatically?

options.text: The statement concerns an assessment of transmission.
The exact report under discussion should be identified.
Every wording attributed to that report, including later additions, is thereby authenticated.
The scope of the specialist's wording matters.

questions.explanation: Assess additions separately.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: Why is it inaccurate to label every weak report fabricated?

options.text: Every weak report is necessarily sound.
Fabrication refers only to spelling mistakes.
Weak and fabricated are always interchangeable labels.
Weakness may arise from a transmission problem without proof that the report was invented.

questions.explanation: Weakness need not mean invention.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: Several transmission routes appear to support a report. What must be checked before claiming that their number strengthens it?

options.text: Their independence and the nature of their defects
Only the number of social-media accounts quoting them
Whether all routes use the same font
Whether the conclusion would be emotionally pleasing

questions.explanation: Comparing routes requires more than counting them.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: A report is classified as ahad. Which statement avoids confusing transmission quantity with authenticity?

options.text: Ahad automatically means fabricated.
It still needs assessment and can be accepted or rejected depending on the evidence.
Ahad automatically means every wording is beyond examination.
Ahad is simply another name for a Quranic verse.

questions.explanation: Ahad reports include accepted and rejected reports.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: Two accepted narrations appear to conflict. What should precede declaring that one has been abrogated?

options.text: Select the one that matches personal preference.
Assume the shorter one must be later.
Examine whether they can be reconciled in context.
Declare both fabricated immediately.

questions.explanation: Consider reconciliation first.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: Why is knowing which report is later important to a specific claim of abrogation?

options.text: A report's page number always establishes its date.
The less popular report must be earlier.
A reader's preference determines historical order.
Supersession requires an established later instruction, not an assumed sequence.

questions.explanation: Sequence requires evidence.

references.label: Ibn Hajar: Nukhbat al-Fikr, sections on transmission, accepted reports and defects

questions.question: A saying contains sound advice, but its prophetic attribution has not been established. Which presentation is most responsible?

options.text: Present the advice without claiming the Prophet said it, while investigating the attribution.
Declare it authentic because its advice is good.
Invent a chain to preserve the lesson.
Say its meaning removes any need for a source.

questions.explanation: Truthful advice and truthful attribution are distinct responsibilities; the warning against false attribution remains relevant.

questions.question: A narration in Muslim's Introduction records Ibn Sirin's own statement about checking sources. Who should be credited with that statement?

options.text: The Prophet automatically, because it appears in a hadith book
Ibn Sirin, unless separate evidence establishes prophetic attribution
The translator as the original speaker
Any companion chosen by the reader

questions.explanation: A collection can contain scholarly statements as well as prophetic reports. The cited passage explicitly attributes this statement to Ibn Sirin.

references.label: Sahih Muslim, Introduction 26: statement of Ibn Sirin (in-book narration 25)

questions.question: A reader finds one authentic narration and immediately issues a complex legal verdict without training. What distinction matters?

options.text: An authentic report never has any legal significance.
A translation alone eliminates the need for context.
Establishing a report's authenticity and deriving a ruling are different tasks.
Every reader's first legal conclusion is equally authoritative.

questions.explanation: Authenticity does not remove the need for interpretation and relevant evidence.

references.label: Sunnah.com: About Hadith; sources and numbering

questions.question: Two qualified specialists give different grades to a report. What should a careful learner preserve when recording the disagreement?

options.text: Only whichever grade is more convenient
An invented claim that all specialists agree
A conclusion that hadith study has no methods
Who graded it, the exact report or route assessed, and each stated judgment

questions.explanation: A grading belongs to a particular assessment; comparing evidence is more careful than erasing the disagreement.

references.label: Abu Dawud: Letter to the People of Makkah, discussion of collection methods and assessments

questions.question: Someone quotes only an encouraging part of Sahih al-Bukhari 3461 and omits its fabrication warning. Which response best preserves the report's meaning?

options.text: Read the encouragement together with the warning rather than turning permission to convey into permission to invent.
Assume encouragement cancels every warning in the same narration.
Treat the omitted warning as a translator's decorative note.
Conclude that adding false sayings is recommended if they inspire people.

questions.explanation: Selective quotation should not reverse the responsibility that the full narration establishes.

questions.question: Sahih al-Bukhari 7352 mentions reward for a judge who strives to reach a judgment but errs. Which inference exceeds what the report itself establishes?

options.text: The narration distinguishes a correct judgment from an erroneous one.
Any untrained person is guaranteed reward for guessing a religious ruling.
The report concerns a judge exercising judgment.
A mistake and a correct conclusion are not described identically.

questions.explanation: The report concerns striving in judgment; it is not an unrestricted endorsement of uninformed guessing.

questions.question: In Sahih Muslim 2577a, the Prophet narrates a message from his Lord. What feature makes this a clear example of hadith qudsi?

options.text: The report becomes a numbered Quranic ayah.
The narration has no transmitters.
The Prophet explicitly reports words from Allah.
The message was composed by its English translator.

questions.explanation: This report is transmitted as hadith with attribution to Allah; it is not thereby part of the Quran.

questions.question: After sharing a saying as hadith, a person discovers that the attribution was false. What best serves truthful transmission?

options.text: Leave it unchanged because correcting it may be embarrassing.
Replace its source with an unrelated authentic hadith number.
Continue sharing it while privately admitting the problem.
Correct the attribution clearly where it was shared and stop circulating it as prophetic.

questions.explanation: The prohibition of false attribution supports correcting a known error rather than preserving its circulation.
